chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Businessmen control pop; artists were once backed
summary: Wilson argues advertising and business-school planners now shape public taste, whereas in the thirties Hammond backed artists; he spent three hours on one solo take in 1935.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well, we're hoping -- I mean, in America, everything is sold -- advertising. We can sell anything, but also, Madison Avenue and the people in power, they can take almost anything -- they can take any dumb artist, any young person, and with a proper amount of publicity, you see what they can do.
Now these are all the businessmen who are in control who do that.

They control the public taste through the advertising thing, and then they control the production of the product, but they can condition the buyer, too. See, it's all in the hands of the businessman now.

So a talented person -- all he can do is come in where they need him and take orders and be told what to do, whereas years ago back in the thirties, a lot of times, the businessman would tell the talented person, well, you go ahead and I will back you on what you're doing -- what you believe in. You know, like John Hammond got behind us back there.
And let me work on one tune, I worked

on solo records back in 1935 for three hours just for one song. You can't do that now. I would just go over and over it again until I got a take that I liked. But that's the businessman going along with the artist, you know?

But now, the artist is told what to do, when to lay out, and the businessman plans the whole thing and you have your computers and his graphs and charts and Cashbox and Billboards, studying waves and trends and fashions and what the other guys sell, maybe we can duplicate it, we can do a little takeoff on that, and think only in terms of profits.
It didn't used to be like that, Teddy.

The talent is just a small part of the whole structure, which is conditioning the public from the beginning and then furnishing the product, and you got control of the public taste, right through the production, distribution and sale, and through the advertising agency, the business people are in the saddle now with the whole thing. I think with pop music now, I think pop music is their product now, it's not the product of the musicians or artistic people, it's the product of these guys from the business schools of Harvard and MIT and they got their electronic computers now, and they can - like insurance companies, they can quote
statistics and everything, what the sales of a certain music are, just like a guy plotting the sale of cigarettes or any other commodity. It's in the hands of those kinds of people.
